facts.claim: Kohavi et al. (2009): in an A/B test users are randomly exposed to the control or the treatment, and no factor may influence who gets which, so a properly run test’s differences are caused by the change.
Kohavi et al. (2009): an A/A test splits users into two groups but shows both the same experience; at a 95% confidence level it should declare a difference about 5% of the time.
Kohavi et al. (2009): a confidence level, commonly 95%, means that 5% of the time a test concludes there is a difference when there is none.
Kohavi et al. (2009): power, commonly wanted at around 80–95%, is the chance a real difference is found significant; more users, usually a longer test, raise it.
Kohavi et al. (2009) give a rule of thumb, 16σ²/Δ² users per variant for 95% confidence and 80% power: for 5% conversion and a 5% change in it, under 122,000 users.
Johari et al. (KDD 2017): users of A/B testing software watch results continuously while a test runs, and then the usual p-values and confidence intervals give unreliable inference.
Johari, Pekelis and Walsh’s “Always Valid Inference” brings sequential analysis to A/B testing, so a test can be monitored continuously and still be read correctly.
Kohavi et al. (2009): decide the comparison in advance, or results that look significant by chance get likelier; corrections such as Bonferroni’s raise the bar and lower power.
Benjamini and Hochberg (1995) proposed controlling the false discovery rate, the expected share of wrongly rejected hypotheses, a gentler bar than guarding against any false finding.
Kohavi et al. (2009): a good overall criterion is not short-term; with revenue alone you might plaster ads over a page, though many ads hurt the user experience.
Kohavi and Longbotham’s checklist for reading an experiment asks whether guardrail metrics warn about unusual differences between the variants.
